xu.summary: The preface tells the life of the Dharma master Duanfu, whose pagoda this is: his birth and family, his ordination and study of the sutras, vinaya and treatises, the favour shown by Emperors Dezong, Shunzong and Xianzong, his direction of monastic affairs at court, and his death in the first year of Kaicheng, when relics were enshrined in the pagoda. It ends by explaining why his disciples asked for this text.
xu.translation:
The Xuanmi Pagoda is where the spirit-bones of the great Dharma master Duanfu came to rest. Ah! A man of stature, living at home, spreads humaneness, rightness, ritual and music, and helps the Son of Heaven to support the age and guide its customs; having left home, he practises compassion, concentration and wisdom, and helps the Tathagata to make the teaching clear and benefit living beings. Without this one cannot be a man of stature, and turning away from this one cannot reach the Way. The master was surely the hero among those who have left home!

He was of the Zhao family of Tianshui, which had lived in Qin for generations. At first, his mother, Lady Zhang, dreamed of an Indian monk who said to her: "You will bear a noble son." He took a relic out of his bag and made her swallow it. When the child was born, the monk of her dream came into her room in broad daylight, stroked the child's head and said: "He will surely spread the teaching greatly." When he had spoken he vanished. Grown up, the master had a high forehead and deep-set eyes, a broad jaw and a square mouth; he was six chi and five cun tall, and his voice was like a bell. One who is to bear the bodhi of the Tathagata and open the ears and eyes of living beings must surely have extraordinary signs and marks!

At ten he took the novice's vows under the Chan master Daowu of Chongfu Temple. At seventeen he was properly ordained as a monk (bhikshu), and belonged to Anguo Temple. He learned the full conduct of a monk from the vinaya master Zhao at Ximing Temple, and received the rules of what to keep and what is a breach from the vinaya master Sheng at Chongfu Temple. The great meaning of the Consciousness-Only teaching he took from the master Su at Anguo Temple, and the main idea of the Nirvana Sutra from the master Yin at Fulin Temple. Again he dreamed of an Indian monk who filled a glass vessel with relics and made him swallow them, saying: "The great teaching of the Three Baskets is all stored in your belly now." From then on, in the sutras, the vinaya and the treatises he had no equal in the world. He took them in like a river gathering streams, found the source wherever he met it and joined the end to the beginning; in broad flood, none could cross to his shore. One who wants to cut down the stumps in the field of feeling and rain sweet dew on the seeds of the Dharma must surely have courage, wisdom and great eloquence!

Before long he visited Manjushri at Qingliang, where all the holy ones appeared; he expounded the great sutra at Taiyuan, and the whole city gathered to hear him. Emperor Dezong heard his name and summoned him, and was greatly pleased at the first meeting. He often went in and out of the palace, discussing with Confucians and Daoists. He was granted the purple robe, and gifts every season, different from those of the others. Again he was commanded to attend the Crown Prince in the Eastern Court. Emperor Shunzong deeply admired his manner and treated him as close as a brother; they slept and rose together, and his favour and courtesy were especially high. Emperor Xianzong visited his temple several times, treating him as a guest and friend. He was often consulted, and his counsel was received with special weight. The master's bearing was lofty, his words and reasoning quick as echoes; in meeting the emperor's wishes he always fitted the true vehicle. Even in a hasty answer he never failed to make the teaching clear. Thus the Son of Heaven came more and more to know that the Buddha is a great sage, and that his teaching holds great inconceivable things.

In those days the court was subduing and levelling the realm, binding Wu, wresting back Shu, flooding Cai and sweeping Yun, while the Son of Heaven sat with folded hands, with nothing to do. He commanded the master to lead the black-robed monks to welcome the true bone relic of the Buddha from the holy mountain (the Famen Temple), and to open a Dharma ground in the secret hall to seek blessings for the people, and himself offered incense and lamps. Afterwards punishments were not cruel, armies were not abused, the people had no sound of grief, and the blue sea had no startling waves. This was a clear proof of how the true teaching, used alongside, assists great government. One who wants to show the great inconceivable way and help a lord who does great things must surely have a hidden tally and a dark accord!

For ten years in all he was in charge of the ritual of the inner halls and kept the records of monks' affairs for the Left Street, setting an example for the pure assembly. He gave lectures on the Nirvana Sutra and the Consciousness-Only treatises, taking on the duty as head of the school to guide monks and laity, and these came to a hundred and sixty sessions. He practised the three secrets in yoga and accorded with non-arising in siddhi. He recited the various sections of texts day by day, more than a hundred thousand times. He pointed to the Pure Land as the place where he would put down his burden, and adorned golden sutras to repay the grace of the Dharma. The offerings given to him, tens or hundreds of myriads in all, he used entirely to adorn halls, with the utmost carving and painting; while in his own abbot's room, on a simple cot, he found calm thought for himself. Noble ministers and great families all relied on and admired him; the bold, the artisans and the merchants all looked up to him. They offered gold and treasures to show their sincerity, looked up to his dignified countenance and bowed at his feet, a thousand in a day, more than can be written down. And the master, seeing the Buddha in all living beings, left behind the four marks and practised good; his heart was low as the ground, level, without hill or ridge. Princes and lords, carriage-bearers and servants all received the same sincerity. Critics said that the one who accomplished the practice of the Never-Disparaging bodhisattva was the master alone. One who wants to steer the great ship that crosses the sea and rescue those lost on the road to the other shore must surely have rare merit and a wondrous Way!

On the first day of the sixth month of the first year of Kaicheng, he passed away, lying on his right side facing west. In the summer heat his noble face was as if alive, and all night a strange fragrance still hung in the air. On the sixth day of the seventh month of that year he was moved to the southern plain of Changle, and, as he had left in his will, was cremated, and more than three hundred relic grains were obtained. When the fire burned strongly, the spirit light was bright as the moon; when it was ashes, the spirit bones were round as pearls. He was granted the posthumous title "Greatly Penetrating" and the pagoda was named "Xuanmi". His age in the world was sixty-seven, and his monastic years were forty-eight. His disciples, monks and nuns together, were about a thousand: some lectured on the dark words, some managed great temples, some cultivated meditation and held to the vinaya. Fifty of them became teachers of men, and all his pupils were men of penetration. Ah! Was the master not truly the hero among those who have left home? If not, how could such supreme virtue and rare signs be so abundant?

The disciples who inherited his work, Yijun, Zizheng, Zhengyan and others, are able to carry on the work of their predecessor and reverently keep his surviving manner. They greatly feared that his fine achievements would one day be buried. And the present Gate Commissioner, Lord Liu, whose Dharma bond is deepest and whose accord with the Way is firmest, also made the request, wishing to spread the fame of the pure dust. I, Xiu, once wandered in his enclosure and knew his affairs; rejoicing in them and praising him, I have words that I need not be ashamed of.

keyLines.line: 玄祕塔者，大法師端甫靈骨之所歸也
keyLines.en: The Xuanmi Pagoda is where the spirit-bones of the great Dharma master Duanfu came to rest
keyLines.note: The opening names the subject: this pagoda holds the remains of the master Duanfu.

keyLines.line: 為丈夫者，在家則張仁義禮樂，輔天子以扶世導俗；出家則運慈悲定慧，佐如來以闡教利生
keyLines.en: A man of stature, living at home, spreads humaneness, rightness, ritual and music and helps the Son of Heaven; having left home, he practises compassion, concentration and wisdom and helps the Tathagata
keyLines.note: The author's view of life: whether at home or as a monk, one can be a man of stature.

keyLines.en: He was of the Zhao family of Tianshui, which had lived in Qin for generations
keyLines.note: Gives Duanfu's family: the Zhao of Tianshui, long settled in the old land of Qin.

keyLines.en: In the sutras, the vinaya and the treatises he had no equal in the world
keyLines.note: Says Duanfu mastered all three baskets of the Buddhist canon so completely that none could match him.

keyLines.line: 德宗皇帝聞其名，徵之，一見大悅
keyLines.en: Emperor Dezong heard his name and summoned him, and was greatly pleased at the first meeting
keyLines.note: Records the summons from Emperor Dezong, after which Duanfu enjoyed imperial favour.

keyLines.line: 以開成元年六月一日，西向右脅而滅
keyLines.en: On the first day of the sixth month of the first year of Kaicheng, he passed away, lying on his right side facing west
keyLines.note: The time and posture of his death: the first day of the sixth month of 836, lying on his right side, facing west.

keyLines.en: He was granted the posthumous title 'Greatly Penetrating' and the pagoda was named 'Xuanmi'
keyLines.note: The court gave him the title Da Da, and the pagoda was named Xuanmi, which is where the stele's name comes from.

keyLines.line: 休嘗遊其藩，備其事，隨喜讚歎，蓋無愧辭
keyLines.en: I, Xiu, once visited his enclosure and came to know his affairs; I rejoice and praise him with words that I am not ashamed of
keyLines.note: The author, Pei Xiu, says he knew Duanfu personally, and this is what his account rests on.

glossary.note: The bones, or relics, left after the cremation of an eminent monk.
A man who has taken the ten precepts and left home but is not yet twenty.
A man fully ordained under the complete precepts.
The whole Buddhist canon: sutras, vinaya (monastic rules) and treatises.

glossary.en: ci zi - being granted the purple
glossary.note: In the Tang dynasty (618-907) the emperor gave a purple robe to a monk of great merit, a mark of honour.

glossary.en: cha pi - cremation (also read tu pi)

glossary.note: The number of years since a monk was ordained.
The crystal-like bone pieces left after the cremation of an eminent monk.

xu.background: The Xuanmi Pagoda Stele has the full title 'Stele Inscription with Preface for the Pagoda of the Great Dharma Master Da Da of Anguo Temple, ...' and was set up in the first year of Huichang (841). Pei Xiu wrote the text and Liu Gongquan wrote it out; it is kept in the Forest of Steles in Xi'an. Liu Gongquan's regular script is strong and sinewy and is known as the 'Liu style'; with Ouyang Xun, Yan Zhenqing and Zhao Mengfu he is counted among the four great masters of regular script.

ming.summary: The inscription is in four-character rhymed lines. It sums up what Duanfu did for the teaching: he sorted out the sutras, vinaya and treatises, refuted false doctrines and walked freely in the world without being stained. It laments that the death of this eminent monk is like the fall of a main beam, leaving later students lingering in admiration.
ming.translation:
Of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadra kalpa,
the fourth is the Sage of Humaneness.
Pitying living beings,
he brought forth the sutras to break up the dust.
The net of the teaching is spread high;
who can tell one strand from another?
There is a great Dharma master
as if he had heard it from the Buddha himself.
The sutras, the vinaya and the treatises,
the trainings in precepts, concentration and wisdom -
deep or shallow, they share one source,
and earlier and later awaken one another.
Strange schools and one-sided meanings:
which is right and which is wrong?
There is a great Dharma master
who made himself frost and hail against them.
Go towards truth and you are stuck;
wade into the world and you are swept away.
The elephant is wild and the ape is light;
hooks and cages cannot hold them.
With the brake set and the blade cutting,
sores and warts still grow.
There is a great Dharma master
who wanders free of thought.
The great Tang opens a new age,
and the Great Hero sends down his teaching.
A thousand years of hidden accord;
the Three Vehicles shine in turn.
With deep honour and favour,
he made the teaching clear and led with praise.
There is a great Dharma master
who met his time and answered the call.
The empty gate has just been rightly opened,
the Dharma hall newly thrown wide;
the lofty beams and rafters
fall in a single day.
Moon in water, image in a mirror:
no mind, coming and going.
He leaves only those who learn after him
gazing up and lingering.

keyLines.en: There is a great Dharma master, as if he had heard it from the Buddha himself
keyLines.note: The line 'there is a great Dharma master' returns again and again, each time praising a different achievement of Duanfu.

glossary.en: xian jie - the Bhadra kalpa (the Auspicious Aeon)
glossary.note: In Buddhist teaching, the present age, in which a thousand buddhas are to appear.

glossary.en: neng ren - the Sage of Humaneness
glossary.note: A rendering of the meaning of Shakyamuni.

glossary.en: jing lu lun zang - the baskets of sutras, vinaya and treatises
glossary.note: The three divisions of the Buddhist canon.

glossary.en: jie ding hui - precepts, concentration, wisdom
glossary.note: The three trainings of Buddhism: keeping the precepts, meditation and wisdom.
The vehicles of the hearers, the solitary realisers and the bodhisattvas; broadly, the different paths of practice.
In old times a block of wood used to stop a cart, here meaning to hold in check. Pronounced ni.

glossary.en: shui yue jing xiang - moon in water, image in a mirror
glossary.note: A figure meaning that all things are like the moon in water or a face in a mirror, unreal and empty.

ming.background: This is the inscription part of the Xuanmi Pagoda Stele, written by Pei Xiu and copied by Liu Gongquan. The stele was completed in the first year of Huichang (841).
